documentNotes.title: INSTRUCTIONS
documentNotes.statement:
DO NOT OPEN THIS TEST UNTIL YOU ARE TOLD TO BEGIN

- Show all your work. Partial credit will be given.
- Start each question on a new sheet of paper. Be sure to put your name in the upper right-hand corner of each page, along with the question number and the page number/total pages for this problem. For example, Doe, Jamie / Q1 – 1/3
- A hand-held calculator may be used. Its memory must be cleared of data and programs. You may use only the basic functions found on a simple scientific calculator. Calculators may not be shared. You may not use any tables, books, or collections of formulas.
- Each of the four questions is worth 25 points. The questions are not necessarily of the same difficulty.

**Possibly Useful Information**

Gravitational field at the Earth’s surface $g=9.8\ N/kg$

Newton’s gravitational constant $G=6.67\times10^{-11}\ N\cdot m^2/kg^2$

Binomial expansion $(1+x)^n\approx1+nx$ for $|x|\ll1$

Moment of Inertia about Center of Mass – Uniform Object (will not be provided on the second screening exam)

| Object | Moment of Inertia |
| --- | --- |
| Disk | $\frac12MR^2$ |
| Sphere | $\frac25MR^2$ |
| Rod | $\frac1{12}ML^2$ |

documentNotes.statement: Any correct solution should be awarded equivalent points. Suggested partial-credit points are presented in square brackets at the right margin. You may further break down the listed points into one point increments. If it is clear they have done an intermediate step, they should get credit for it even if they have not presented it. For example, in 1.a., if a student wrote down $mv_0r_0=mvr$, they should get 6 points credit. Students should not be penalized in a subsequent part for using the wrong answer to a previous part. (No double jeopardy.)

problems.statement:
A mass $m$ attached to a massless string moves around a circle of radius $r_0$ with speed $v_0$ on a frictionless table as shown in the accompanying diagram. The string passes through a small hole in the table. Starting at time $t=0$, the string is pulled downward with a constant speed $V$. Determine:

![Mass on a table moving around a hole while the string is pulled downward](#p1-fig1)

parts.label: a
parts.statement: The tangential speed $v$ of mass $m$ as a function of $r$.

parts.label: b
parts.statement: The tangential speed $v$ of mass $m$ as a function of time $t$.

parts.label: c
parts.statement: The force needed to pull the string as a function of time $t$.

parts.label: d
parts.statement: The work done on the mass by the string from time $t=0$ to time $t$.

solution.statement:
**a.** The string force on the mass acts in the radial direction. It exerts no torque, so angular momentum is conserved. $L_0=L$ [2]

For a particle of mass $m$ moving with speed $v$ in a circle of radius $r$, the angular momentum is

$$L=mvr.$$

[2]

Equating the angular momentum at time $t=0$ to that at time $t$

$$mv_0r_0=mvr.$$

[2]

Solving for $v$

$$v=\frac{v_0r_0}{r}.\qquad\text{Eq. 1-1}$$

[1]

**b.** The string and attached mass are pulled with constant speed $V$ radially inward

$$-V=\frac{\Delta r}{\Delta t}=\frac{r-r_0}{t-0},$$

[2]

where the radially outward direction has been chosen to be positive.

$$r=r_0-Vt.\qquad\text{Eq. 1-2}$$

[2]

Substituting this into Eq. 1-1 above

$$v=\frac{v_0r_0}{(r_0-Vt)}\qquad\text{Eq. 1-3}$$

[2]

**c.** Since the string is massless, the net force acting on it is zero. [1]

Denoting the force needed to pull the string by $F$ and the tension in the string by $T$,

$$F=T,$$

[1]

The string tension $T$ supplies the centripetal force acting on the mass

$$F=m\frac{v^2}{r}.$$

[2]

Substituting $v$ and $r$ from Eq. 1-3 and Eq. 1-2,

$$F=m\frac{v_0^2r_0^2}{(r_0-Vt)^3}$$

[2]

**d.** Using the work-energy theorem

$$W_{net}=\Delta K$$

[2]

$$W_{net}=\frac12mv^2-\frac12mv_0^2$$

[2]

Combining with Eq. 1-3

$$W_{net}=\frac12m\left(\frac{v_0r_0}{r_0-Vt}\right)^2-\frac12mv_0^2=\frac12mv_0^2\left(\frac{r_0^2}{(r_0-Vt)^2}-1\right).$$

[2]

figures.alt: Mass on a table moving around a hole while the string is pulled downward

problems.statement: Two twin asteroids of identical mass $M$ are located a distance $r$ apart. A probe of mass $m$ (with $m\ll M$) is released from rest a distance $A$ (with $A\ll r$) from the center of mass of the two-body asteroid system. The probe is an equal distance from both asteroids. Assume that the probe does not affect the separation distance $r$ and that all other objects in the universe are too far away to exert a significant gravitational force. The asteroids must be orbiting their common center of mass in order to maintain a constant distance, but ignore any effects of orbiting in this problem. For both parts, clearly justify any approximations that you are making and give your answers in terms of $r$, $A$, $G$, $M$, and $m$.

parts.label: a
parts.statement: How long will it take for the probe to reach the center of mass?

parts.label: b
parts.statement: What will be the speed of the probe as it passes through the center of mass of the asteroid system?

solution.statement:
(If a student's only error is using $r$ instead of $r/2$ as the asteroid to center of mass distance, deduct only one point for part a) and one point for part b).)

**a.** Let $x$ = the distance of the probe from the center of mass of the asteroid system. The diagram below is not to scale. The distance $x$ has been greatly exaggerated. The probe is released from $A=x_{max}$. Diagram [3]

![Probe displaced from the midpoint between two asteroids and the two gravitational forces](#p2-sol-fig1)

The magnitude of the force $F$ that each asteroid exerts on the probe is

$$F=\frac{GMm}{(r/2)^2+x^2}.\qquad\text{Eq. 2-1}$$

[2]

The total force on the probe is in the negative $x$-direction and equal to [1]

$$F_x=-2F\sin\theta\qquad\text{Eq. 2-2}$$

[1]

with

$$\sin\theta=\frac{x}{\sqrt{(r/2)^2+x^2}}\qquad\text{Eq. 2-3}$$

[1]

combining Eqs. 2-1, 2-2, 2-3

$$F_x=-2G\frac{Mm}{(r/2)^2+x^2}\frac{x}{\sqrt{(r/2)^2+x^2}}=-\frac{2GMmx}{\left((r/2)^2+x^2\right)^{3/2}}$$

[1]

Since $x\le A\ll r$,

$$\left((r/2)^2+x^2\right)^{3/2}=\left((r/2)^2\right)^{3/2}\left(1+(2x/r)^2\right)^{3/2}\approx(r/2)^3.$$

[1]

With this approximation, $F_x$ becomes

$$F_x\approx-\frac{16GMm}{r^3}x$$

[1]

Comparing this with the defining equation of simple harmonic motion $F=-kx$ [1]

(Students should be given equivalent credit for a valid method using calculus.)

The motion is approximately simple harmonic with

$$k=\frac{16GMm}{r^3}\qquad\text{Eq. 2-4}$$

[1]

The period of simple harmonic motion is

$$T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}\qquad\text{Eq. 2-5}$$

[1]

Combining Eqs. 2-4 and 2-5

$$T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{(16GMm/r^3)}}=\frac{2\pi}{4}\sqrt{\frac{r^3}{GM}}$$

[1]

The time $t$ for the probe to reach the center of mass of the asteroid system is

$$t=\frac{T}{4}$$

[1]

$$t=\frac{2\pi}{16}\sqrt{\frac{r^3}{GM}}=\frac{\pi}{8}\sqrt{\frac{r^3}{GM}}$$

[1]

**b.** The center of mass of the asteroid system is the equilibrium position for the simple harmonic motion. The probe's velocity as it passes through the equilibrium position is

$$v_{max}=\omega x_{max}=\omega A.$$

[2]

$$\omega=\frac{2\pi}{T}$$

[2]

$$\omega=\frac{2\pi}{(2\pi/4)\sqrt{r^3/GM}}=4\sqrt{\frac{GM}{r^3}}.$$

[2] Then

$$v_{max}=4A\sqrt{\frac{GM}{r^3}}.$$

[2]

figures.alt: Probe displaced from the midpoint between two asteroids and the two gravitational forces

problems.statement: In this problem, please use $g=10\ N/kg$. A bead of mass $0.050\ kg$ is placed on a long vertical wire which is firmly attached to both the floor and ceiling. As the bead slides on the wire the magnitude of the frictional force between the bead and the wire is a constant $0.20\ N$. The bead is released from rest at an initial height of $1.47\ m$ above the floor. Assume all collisions with the floor are perfectly elastic and that air resistance can be neglected.

parts.label: a
parts.statement: What is the bead's greatest height after colliding with the floor?

parts.label: b
parts.statement: How much time does it take the bead to slide from its initial height of $1.47\ m$ to the floor?

parts.label: c
parts.statement: How much time does it take the bead to travel from the floor to the height found in a) above?

parts.label: d
parts.statement: What is the total distance the bead travels before coming to rest?

solution.statement:
$m=0.050\ kg$, $mg=(0.050\ kg)(10\ m/s^2)=0.50\ N$, $h=1.47\ m$, $f=0.20\ N$.

**a.** Use the work energy theorem

$$W_{nc}=\Delta K+\Delta U\qquad\text{Eq. 3-1}$$

[2] where $W_{nc}$ is the work done by the non-conservative frictional force, $\Delta K$ is the change in kinetic energy, and $\Delta U$ is the change in potential energy. Let $h'$ = greatest height after colliding with the floor. We will compare energies at the initial height $h$ and the final height $h'$. The frictional force is always opposite to the direction of motion, so the work done is the negative of the frictional force times the total distance traveled.

$$W_{nc}=-f(h+h')$$

[2]

$$\Delta K=0$$

[1]

$$\Delta U=mg(h'-h)$$

[2] Combining with Eq. 3-1,

$$-f(h+h')=mg(h'-h)$$

[1] and solving for $h'$, $(mg+f)h'=(mg-f)h$,

$$h'=h\left(\frac{mg-f}{mg+f}\right)=(1.47\ m)\left(\frac{0.50\ N-0.20\ N}{0.50\ N+0.20\ N}\right)=0.63\ m.$$

[1]

**b.** As the bead moves downward, the frictional force is upward. Choosing the downward (acceleration) direction to be positive and the origin of the coordinate system to be at the point of release, we have $\sum F=ma$. [1]

$$mg-f=ma$$

[1]

$$a=\frac{mg-f}{m}=\frac{0.50\ N-0.20\ N}{0.050\ kg}=6.0\ m/s^2$$

[1]

$$y=y_0+v_0t+\frac12at^2$$

[1] with $y=h=1.47\ m$, $y_0=0$, and $v_0=0$:

$$t=\sqrt{\frac{2h}{a}}=\sqrt{\frac{2(1.47\ m)}{6.0\ m/s^2}}=0.70\ s.$$

[2]

**c.** In order to find the initial velocity after the bounce, find the final velocity of the bead immediately before the bounce.

$$v=v_0+at=0+(6.0\ m/s^2)(0.70\ s)=4.2\ m/s\quad\text{(downward)}.$$

[1] Since the collision with the floor is elastic, the initial velocity of the bead after the bounce is $v_0=-4.2\ m/s$ (upward). [1]

As the bead moves upward $\sum F=ma$.

The frictional force is downward $mg+f=ma$ [1]

$$a=\frac{mg+f}{m}=\frac{0.50\ N+0.20\ N}{0.050\ kg}=14.0\ m/s^2.$$

[1] At the highest point, $v=0$, and

$$t=\frac{v-v_0}{a}=\frac{0-(-4.2\ m/s)}{14.0\ m/s^2}=0.30\ s.$$

[1]

**d.** Use the work energy theorem $W_{nc}=\Delta K+\Delta U$. [1] where $W_{nc}$ is the work done by the non-conservative frictional force, $\Delta K$ is the change in kinetic energy, and $\Delta U$ is the change in potential energy. We will compare energies at the initial height $h$ and the final height $0$. Let $s$ = total distance traveled. The work done by the frictional force is the negative of the frictional force times the total distance traveled.

$$W_{nc}=-fs$$

[1]

$$\Delta K=0,\qquad\Delta U=0-mgh$$

[1] Combining $-fs=-mgh$ [1] and solving for $s$

$$s=\frac{mgh}{f}=\frac{(0.50\ N)(1.47\ m)}{0.20\ N}=3.7\ m.$$

[1]

problems.statement:
![Two projectiles launched at 30 degrees and 45 degrees from sites separated by S](#p4-fig1)

A projectile is launched in a vertical plane from a fixed site. It has an initial velocity $v_0$ at an angle of $45^\circ$ above the horizontal. A second projectile is simultaneously launched at an angle of $30^\circ$ from a second site a distance $S$ directly behind the first one. See diagram above. They collide when the first projectile attains its maximum height. Ignore any effects of air resistance. Express your answers in terms of in terms of $v_0$ and $g$.

parts.label: a
parts.statement: Find the separation $S$ between the two launch sites. Hint: You will first need to find the initial velocity of the second projectile.

parts.label: b
parts.statement: What are the velocities of the two projectiles immediately before they collide? (You may leave your answers to this part and the following part in component form.)

parts.label: c
parts.statement: Assuming that the two projectile are identical small spheres of equal mass that collide elastically, what are the velocities of the two spheres immediately after they collide?

solution.statement:
**a.** The two projectiles are simultaneously launched at $t=0$ from $x_{20}=0$, $y_{20}=0$ and $x_{10}=S$, $y_{10}=0$. Let $u_0$ = the initial velocity of the second projectile. The components of the initial velocities are

$$v_{0x}=v_0\cos45^\circ=\frac{v_0}{\sqrt2},\qquad v_{0y}=v_0\sin45^\circ=\frac{v_0}{\sqrt2}$$

[1]

$$u_{0x}=u_0\cos30^\circ=u_0\frac{\sqrt3}{2},\qquad u_{0y}=u_0\sin30^\circ=\frac{u_0}{2}.$$

[1] Projectile 1 reaches its highest point when $v_y=0$. [1]

$$v_y=v_{0y}-gt$$

[1] or

$$t=\frac{v_{0y}}{g}=\frac{v_0}{g\sqrt2}.$$

[1] At this time, $x_1=x_2$ and $y_1=y_2$. [2] With

$$y=y_0+v_{0y}t-\frac12gt^2$$

[1] and $x=x_0+v_{0x}t$. [1] Equating $y$'s at time $t$,

$$y_{10}+v_{0y}t-\frac12gt^2=y_{20}+u_{0y}t-\frac12gt^2$$

[1]

$$v_{0y}t=u_{0y}t$$

[1] Thus $u_0=\sqrt2v_0$. [1] Equating $x$'s at time $t$,

$$x_{10}+v_{0x}t=x_{20}+u_{0x}t.$$

[1] Substituting in for $t$ and $v_0$'s,

$$S+\frac{v_0}{\sqrt2}\left(\frac{v_0}{g\sqrt2}\right)=0+u_0\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\left(\frac{v_0}{g\sqrt2}\right)$$

$$S+\frac{v_0}{\sqrt2}\left(\frac{v_0}{g\sqrt2}\right)=\sqrt2v_0\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\left(\frac{v_0}{g\sqrt2}\right)$$

[1]

$$S+\frac{v_0^2}{2g}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\frac{v_0^2}{g}$$

$$S=\frac{v_0^2}{2g}(\sqrt3-1).$$

[1]

**b.** The $x$- and $y$-components of the velocity are $v_x=v_{0x}$ and $v_y=v_{0y}-gt$. [1] Therefore

$$v_x=v_{0x}=\frac{v_0}{\sqrt2},\qquad v_y=v_{0y}-gt=\frac{v_0}{\sqrt2}-g\frac{v_0}{g\sqrt2}=0$$

[2] and

$$u_x=u_{0x}=u_0\frac{\sqrt3}{2}=\sqrt2v_0\frac{\sqrt3}{2}=v_0\sqrt{1.5}$$

[1]

$$u_y=u_{0y}-gt=\frac{u_0}{2}-g\frac{v_0}{g\sqrt2}=\frac{v_0\sqrt2}{2}-g\frac{v_0}{g\sqrt2}=0$$

[1] Both projectiles are at their highest points.

**c.** Since immediately before the collision the velocities are totally in the $x$-direction, the collision is one-dimensional. [1] The collision is elastic so total momentum and total kinetic energy are unchanged. [2] Because the masses are equal, this requires the velocities to interchange.

$$v_{Fx}=v_0\sqrt{1.5}$$

[1]

$$u_{Fx}=\frac{v_0}{\sqrt2}.$$

[1]
